fb_caption:
System Design & Software Architecture Explained ⚡ (Git Graph Reel) — Branch & Merge under the hood.

When you think of Git as a distributed system, its core primitives line up with architecture trade-offs:

• Branching (isolation): Creating a branch is like spinning up an isolated execution context. You can evolve features independently without blocking the mainline—similar to deploying behind a feature flag.

• Commit graph (immutable state + auditability): Commits are content-addressed snapshots, forming a DAG. This gives you strong explainability: you can reconstruct “what happened” without guessing.

• Merge (convergence strategy): Merging is reconciliation of divergent histories.
  - Fast-forward merge is effectively “no new reconciliation logic”—it assumes the mainline was not moved.
  - 3-way merge performs explicit reconciliation using a common ancestor (think of it as resolving conflicts with reference context).

• Rebase (history rewrite): Rebasing replays commits onto a new base. It can reduce noise and produce a linear history, but it changes commit identities—so it’s analogous to performing a “history rewrite” with potential coordination costs (and requires discipline with shared branches).

• Production lesson: Pick strategies based on your team’s reliability needs.
  - Prefer merge commits when you want maximum traceability of integration events.
  - Prefer squash/rebase when you want a cleaner change log and your workflow supports deterministic replay.

Interview tip: When asked about system design fundamentals, borrow the Git mental model—define isolated work, immutable state, and deterministic convergence paths.
